title: What are value objects and why does immutability matter?
description: Entity vs value semantics, replacing primitive obsession with self-validating immutable types, and how immutability removes whole bug classes.

data.text: **Question:** What are value objects and why does immutability matter?

**Entities** are identified by a stable id (`Order #1042` is the same order after its address changes). **Value objects** are identified by their value alone — `Money(50, USD)`, `Email("a@b.com")`, `DateRange(from, to)` — and are naturally immutable: you don't change a value, you create a new one. Value objects kill primitive obsession: instead of `decimal amount, string currency` traveling together, a `Money` type carries its own validation (no negative amounts, currency always present) and behavior (`Add`, `ApplyPercentage`). Immutability removes race conditions, makes objects safe to share and cache, and turns bugs into compile errors instead of runtime surprises.

**How to recognize a value object:**
- Two instances with the same components are interchangeable — no identity beyond the values
- It answers "what/ how much / which" — amount, color, address (in some models), coordinate, percentage
- It's small, self-contained, and shared freely

**Signs you need one (primitive obsession symptoms):**
- Validation scattered: `if (amount < 0)` re-checked in five services because the type is just `decimal`
- Parameter twins: methods taking `(string street, string city, string zip, string country)` that always travel together
- Conversion bugs: passing a `decimal` price where a `decimal` percentage was expected — both compile
- Formatting leaking everywhere: every call site re-formats an email/phone/currency its own way

**Why immutable:**
- **No aliasing surprises** — a cached object can't be mutated by whoever holds a reference
- **Thread safety by construction** — no locks needed for shared read-only values
- **Predictable state** — an object's fields can't change between two lines of your method
- **Cheap copies** — copy-on-write and "modified request" patterns become natural

**C# mechanics:** `readonly struct` or `record`/`record struct` gives value equality for free; `init`-only setters allow construction-time validation without mutability; `with` expressions create modified copies. Keep validation in the constructor/factory so an invalid value object cannot exist.

data.title: Primitive obsession vs a Money value object
Where value objects don't belong
data.text: Don't wrap everything. ORM entity keys, simple internal flags, and data-transfer DTOs usually stay primitives — value objects add ceremony with no payoff when there are no invariants or behavior to protect. Reach for one when the same primitive keeps needing the same validation, or when bugs have come from mixing up twin parameters.

Interviewers want to hear:
- Identity vs value semantics as the defining difference from entities
- Concrete benefits: validation in one place, no aliasing bugs, thread-safe sharing
- C# specifics: records, `init`, `with`, readonly structs, value equality for free
- Judgment: knowing when NOT to introduce one

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Entities have identity; values have equivalence — same components = same value
Value objects are immutable, self-validating, and carry their own behavior
They eliminate primitive obsession: twin params, scattered validation, mix-up bugs
C#: records + init-only setters + `with` expressions; don't wrap what has no invariants
data.takeaway: If you validate the same primitive in five places, that validation and the data belong together in a value object.
